Holder briefing

Who checks the decisions?

Examine three different questions: who approves payments, what completion means, and who retains technical control.

Beneficiary participation in approvals

A payment can be formally approved while still raising questions about the independence of that approval. The relevant records identify who proposed, voted and executed, as well as who received funds.

Estima’s kickoff release

The other three directors approved the original A266 grant. 0xphilipp then voted YES on A271, which released its 45,000-USDC kickoff payment. The record therefore distinguishes approval of the grant from approval of a payment benefiting his project.

Superbolt distributions

In P3, 0xphilipp proposed a 7,500-USDC invoice payment and voted YES; the payment followed the next day. P35 allocated 45,000 USDC to 0xphilipp and three 15,000-USDC amounts. Recorded beneficiary YES votes included 0xphilipp, MB and Rebel; MB executed.

Participation differs by decision. In P41, 0xphilipp received a payment but had no recorded vote. The record also documents completed Superbolt milestones; beneficiary involvement does not by itself establish that no work was delivered.

Completion, cost and outcomes

The cited approvals do not provide an itemized cost basis, independent price comparisons or quantified outcome targets. Accepting a milestone as complete does not answer what it should cost or how much value Terra should receive.

The Creda analytics milestone

0xphilipp proposed and voted YES on A215, enabling a 10,000-USDC analytics milestone. The payment was made on 27 January 2026. A preserved capture of the dedicated analytics page on 18 October still displayed placeholders.

That capture is evidence of the page’s state at that date. It does not establish that every part of Creda was absent or that no development work took place.

What the voting record shows

Across A1–A289, MB voted YES on 251 of the 252 0xphilipp proposals on which he cast a ballot. The 23 October 2026 capture combines his earlier and current board wallets.

The one NO was A28, which used the wrong contract. MB voted YES on corrected A29 five minutes and ten seconds later.

Agreement is observable; motive is not established by a tally. Read the ballots alongside the payment relationships when assessing the independence of oversight.

Voting data, transaction links and audit scope

The failed A272 threshold change

A272 proposed removing a director and reducing the approval threshold from 75% to 60%. With three equal seats, 0xphilipp and MB’s two YES votes would have been enough even if the third director voted NO.

Captured configuration

Four equal seats · 75% threshold.
Two YES votes alone are insufficient against two NO votes.

Proposed in A272 · failed

Three equal seats · 60% threshold.
Two YES votes would suffice against one NO.

A272 failed. The captured configuration remained four equal members at 75%. Explicit abstention can affect the denominator; an absent vote is not an abstention. The comparison above assumes the remaining members vote NO.

Technical control is a separate question

The TLA launch terms described handing contract administration to Stewardship after one month and configuration ownership after three. The preserved audit found those powers still held through ERIS wallets.

Using 27 November 2024 as a conservative common cutoff, it identifies 31 privileged operations in 19 successful transactions across seven of the ten original TLA contracts. These included code replacements, registry changes and incentive restrictions.

In his public reply of 19 October 2026, 0xphilipp said ERIS continued to develop, maintain and operate the contracts and considered a transfer inappropriate because of concerns about the board. No replacement authorization for the published deadlines was located in the reviewed record.

That is a bounded finding about the records searched, not proof that an authorization could not exist elsewhere. Board roles, code-migration administration and registry ownership are distinct powers.

What remains to be demonstrated

  • A decision process that addresses beneficiaries’ participation and financial relationships.
  • A cost basis and measurable outcomes for funded milestones.
  • Authorization for retained powers, or executed transfers with each technical role accounted for.
